claims.text: The formation and long-term stability of a protective oxide above 900 °C in CrFeCoNiX alloys is governed by the ability of X to promote crystallographic coherence between the oxide and substrate.
Si is particularly effective at promoting a crystallographically coherent oxide in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Oxide-substrate coherence minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch and growth stresses, thereby preventing oxide cracking and spallation.
The proposed material is a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloy, with X varied among Si, Mn, and Al.
Exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive environment will produce an oxide scale whose evolution can be compared among the Si-, Mn-, and Al-containing alloys.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous oxide phase with a coherent metal/oxide interface, compatible thermal expansion, and retained structural integrity.
Element X controls oxidation kinetics and oxide phase stability by controlling oxide crystallography.
For X = Si, a slow-growing silica-rich oxide forms and bonds well to the substrate.
The silica-rich oxide mitigates stress accumulation at the oxide/substrate interface.
For X = Mn or Al, the resulting oxides are less coherent and have greater volumetric mismatch than the proposed Si-rich oxide.
Poor coherence and volumetric mismatch in the Mn- or Al-containing alloys cause greater growth stress and eventual cracking or spallation.
CrFeCoNiX alloys with sufficient Si will develop a thin, uniform, adherent, and slowly growing oxide scale that resists cracking and spallation.
Comparable CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiAl alloys will exhibit more oxide cracking or spallation because of higher growth stresses and poorer interface coherence.
CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiAl alloys are known to form less-adherent, unstable oxide layers and therefore provide an appropriate baseline.
The proposed comparison is limited to exposure above 900 °C for up to approximately 50–100 hours in controlled oxidative or corrosive environments.
The hypothesis applies only when the alloy remains a metallic solid solution without significant intermetallic formation during exposure.
The Si concentration required to produce the proposed coherent oxide is not known.
Processing conditions and microstructural heterogeneity may affect oxide adhesion and growth.
The hypothesis is falsified if the Si-containing alloy does not form a slower-growing, more coherent, and more adherent scale than the Mn- or Al-containing alloys under equivalent conditions.
The hypothesis is also falsified if the Si-containing alloy shows cracking or spallation equal to or greater than that of the Mn- or Al-containing controls.
